title: Aaron Swartz's legacy lives on, but who profits from it? — Free Software Foundation — Working together for free software
content_html:
— Published on Nov 06, 2026 04:53 PM

November 8 is Aaron Swartz Day, when we remember a pioneer of free software and information sharing whose contributions helped shape the modern internet.

Aaron Swartz would have turned forty this year. In the time since his passing, Swartz's contributions to free software, internet standards, and the freedom to share knowledge have remain enormously important. It is particularly striking that some of the world's largest companies now rely on technology Swartz helped to develop. These companies have used his work in their quest to build proprietary large language models (LLMs), while inviting serious criticism about their own collection and use of copyrighted material. In light of the enormous profits generated from the collection and commercialization of human knowledge in the past year, the contrast between how Swartz was treated in comparison to major technology corporations deserves closer scrutiny.

In 2011, federal prosecutors charged Swartz with computer fraud and related offenses after he downloaded millions of academic articles from the JSTOR collection through MIT's university network. Swartz believed that scholarly knowledge should be available to everyone rather than restricted from access to the public by expensive subscriptions. Although he was not charged with copyright infringement, he faced aggressive federal prosecution and the possibility of decades in prison before he tragically died by suicide in January 2013, at just twenty-six years old.

One of Swartz's most important technical contributions was his collaboration with John Gruber on Markdown, the simple text formatting system introduced in 2004. Markdown allows users to create structured documents using ordinary text, without requiring proprietary software. More than twenty years later, Markdown has become one of the most popular formats for documentation and publishing, and is widely used in community websites such as forums and wikis.

This is not a minor contribution. Companies developing LLMs use Markdown extensively in their products and development tools. OpenAI, for example, recommends Markdown for organizing instructions and communicating structure to its ChatGPT models. Although Markdown is not technically required for LLMs to function, it has become an important part of how people interact with them. A format Swartz helped develop has been adopted across an industry worth trillions of dollars.

Swartz's startup company Infogami merged with Reddit in 2005, making him co-owner of what would become one of the internet's largest collections of online human interactions. Millions of people contributed knowledge, experiences, and opinions to Reddit's communities, with little expectation that their contributions would someday become valuable resources for proprietary LLMs. In 2024, Reddit entered into a reported $60 million annual agreement with Google involving access to its pages for machine learning. That same year, Reddit also announced a partnership with OpenAI, giving the company access to Reddit's data to incorporate into ChatGPT. Information freely contributed by ordinary internet users has become a valuable commercial resource for some of the world's largest technology companies, with little say from the people who contributed to it.

Swartz also developed web.py, a public domain framework for building Python applications, and contributed to RSS 1.0, a public internet standard for distributing news and other information between websites. Python frameworks such as Swartz's work have since become important for collecting and organizing data used in machine learning, and Python is widely used by LLM-based systems such as Claude Code, ChatGPT, and Microsoft's Github Copilot to execute code, analyze data, automate tasks, and generate software.

Structured feeds such as RSS remain important today, allowing millions of users to receive information directly from publishers. RSS also helped give rise to podcasts, enabling independent creators to distribute audio to listeners without needing permission from intermediaries. Although Apple, Spotify, and Google's YouTube have since become dominant forces in this multibillion-dollar industry, podcasting began with decentralized RSS feeds, giving anyone the ability to publish and share media on their own terms. Swartz understood the radical importance of internet standards like RSS, as he made clear in his 2002 Standards Manifesto. That makes the contemporary corporate capture of podcast distribution by proprietary platforms all the more lamentable.

Later technological developments make Swartz's prosecution especially troubling. In 2025, a federal court found that Anthropic had acquired more than seven million unauthorized copies of books from collections including Library Genesis (LibGen) and Pirate Library Mirror. The company subsequently agreed to a $1.5 billion copyright settlement. Meta also downloaded books and academic publications from LibGen and Anna's Archive for training its proprietary Llama models. In May 2026, Elsevier and other major publishers sued Meta, alleging that the company had downloaded millions of copyrighted books and scholarly publications, including material originating from Sci-Hub. In a separate lawsuit, Meta was accused of using BitTorrent to download more than 81.7 terabytes of so-called "pirated" books and academic papers. Because BitTorrent ordinarily involves sharing downloaded data with other users, these allegations raise further questions about the company's role in distributing copyrighted materials.

These cases involve different legal questions, but the enormous scale of the alleged "piracy" by giant technology corporations makes the copying of articles by Swartz look like a proverbial drop in the bucket or, perhaps more accurately, a drop in the ocean. Swartz faced criminal prosecution for downloading academic research that he wanted to distribute with no monetary gain, while corporations have collected vastly larger quantities of books, articles, websites, artwork, software, and public conversations to develop proprietary LLMs. Many of these same corporations have also been criticized by the Federal Trade Commission for their extensive surveillance of internet users.

There is a fundamental contradiction here. Large technology companies benefit from free software, public knowledge, and internet standards developed through decades of collaboration. They rely on technologies like Markdown and Python while restricting what users can do with the products built around them. The knowledge of millions of people becomes part of proprietary systems controlled by a handful of behemoth corporations, which are also utilized for invading the privacy of users.

Free software is ultimately about who controls the technology that shapes our lives and our world. Swartz helped build tools that made the internet more useful and accessible, and his contributions continue to shape a world he never lived to see. On Aaron Swartz Day, we should remember his achievements and the access-to-knowledge principles that guided them. The companies benefiting from his legacy should respect those same principles by giving users true freedom and control, rather than imposing more restrictions on us all.
